content_voiceover: This slide summarizes rhabdomyosarcoma, the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood. Primary sites are distributed across the body, with head and neck accounting for the largest share at about forty percent, followed by the genitourinary tract at around twenty percent, extremities at about twenty percent, and the retroperitoneal region contributing roughly ten percent, trunk sites making up the rest. Pathology and genetics distinguish the two major subtypes. Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma is the unfavorable subtype, driven by a translocation between chromosome two band q thirty-five and chromosome thirteen band q fourteen, and less commonly between chromosome one band q thirty-six and chromosome thirteen band q fourteen, translocations that fuse PAX transcription factor genes to FOXO1. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, the more favorable subtype, is instead characterized by loss of heterozygosity at the eleven p fifteen locus. A cluster of features defines unfavorable risk, advanced pretreatment stage, gross residual disease left after surgery, tumors larger than five centimeters, metastatic disease at diagnosis, alveolar histology itself, an unfavorable primary site, and age older than nine years, since older children have a higher incidence of both advanced disease and alveolar histology. Treatment is multimodal, combining chemotherapy, surgery, and radiotherapy.
keypoints: Most common sites: head and neck, then genitourinary tract and extremities
Alveolar RMS (unfavorable): t(2;13)(q35;q14) or rarely t(1;13)(q36;q14)
Embryonal RMS (favorable): loss of heterozygosity at 11p15
Unfavorable factors: advanced stage, residual disease, tumor over 5 cm, metastasis, alveolar histology, age over 9
Treatment is multimodal: chemotherapy, surgery, and radiotherapy
keypoint_voiceover: Rhabdomyosarcoma splits into alveolar, the unfavorable subtype with a two thirteen translocation, and embryonal, the favorable subtype with eleven p fifteen loss of heterozygosity. Unfavorable features include advanced stage, residual disease, large tumor size, metastasis, and age over nine, and treatment combines chemotherapy, surgery, and radiotherapy.
